The reason for that is that JSON is highly
structured. It stands for JavaScript Object
Notation because it looks like a JavaScript
object in the end. And it's highly
machine-readable whilst also being quite
readable and understandable by humans.
In the end, JSON is just text. It's just
text that has a certain format and follows
certain rules.
And one rule is that we always have wrapping
curly braces.
And in there, we then can have key-value
pairs
where the key names always need to be
between double quotes.
And that's a difference to a regular
JavaScript object. There you don't need
quotes, or if you do use them, you can use
double or single quotes. For JSON, you need
quotes and it needs to be double quotes.
And then you can have your key name,
then a colon, and then your value. For
example, Maximilian if your value is a
string.
You can also have a non-string value like
this number here though. So on the right
side of the colon, you can have other values
than strings. On the left side, your key
names are always strings with double quotes.
You can also have the nested array in there.
And if you then have strings in there,
again, here you also need double quotes. So
if you're working with a string in JSON, it
always needs double quotes.
So that could be my hobbies.
And then we also can have nested objects in
here, and then the same rules as before
apply.
And that's the JSON format. This is the
format in which we'll send the data from

because this format is easy to parse for
both client and server-side code, and
therefore it's the perfect format for
exchanging data.
